name: Pashto (Northwestern dialect)
variety: Northwestern Pashto of the central Ghilzai area (MacKenzie's north-western group; Wardak speech is close to it). Apart from the consonants named below, the description is that of the ps profile.
sources: MacKenzie, D. N. (1959). A standard Pashto. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 22.
Henderson, Michael M. T. (1983). Four varieties of Pashto. Journal of the American Oriental Society 103(3).
Skjærvø, Prods O. (1989). Pashto. In Schmitt (ed.), Compendium Linguarum Iranicarum. Wiesbaden: Reichert.
Tegey, Habibullah and Robson, Barbara (1996). A Reference Grammar of Pashto. Washington: Center for Applied Linguistics.
Elfenbein, Josef (1997). Pashto phonology. In Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa, volume 2. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Robson, Barbara and Tegey, Habibullah (2009). Pashto. In Windfuhr (ed.), The Iranian Languages. London: Routledge.
David, Anne Boyle (2014). Descriptive Grammar of Pashto and its Dialects. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
contrasts: the letters ښ and ږ are palatal fricatives /ç ʝ/, distinct from palato-alveolar /ʃ ʒ/ and from velar /x ɣ/; the southwest has retroflex [ʂ ʐ] for them
ځ is the fricative [z] and so merges with ز; څ is [ts] in most descriptions, with [s] also reported
dental versus retroflex stops /t̪ d̪/ : /ʈ ɖ/, and retroflex nasal /ɳ/ and flap /ɽ/ beside /n/ and /r/
/a/ versus /ə/ versus /ɑ/; /ə/ occurs stressed as well as unstressed
free stress that distinguishes words and grammatical forms
/q f ʔ/ belong to the learned pronunciation of loanwords; everyday speech has [k], [p] and zero
allophony: /ç ʝ/ are palatal fricatives without the retroflex colouring of the southwestern sounds
/ɳ/ is a nasalised retroflex flap [ɽ̃]; it does not begin words
/ɽ/ is a retroflex flap, often with a lateral release
/r/ is an alveolar tap or short trill
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars, [ɳ] before retroflexes and [m] before labials
voiceless stops are unaspirated or only weakly aspirated
/x ɣ/ are velar, with uvular variants next to back vowels
/h/ is weak and is often dropped
phonotactics: many word-initial clusters of two consonants, including ones with falling or level sonority (ʃpa 'night', xwla 'mouth', lmar 'sun', wror 'brother'); a few of three consonants
final clusters of up to two consonants
the short vowels /a ə/ are not written except word-finally, and the spelling is the same as in the other dialects

stress.rule: Stress can fall on any syllable and belongs to the word and to the inflected form: it separates otherwise identical words and the perfective from the imperfective aspect of verbs; as a tendency it falls on the last syllable when that syllable is heavy and otherwise on the penult.
stress.cues: intensity, pitch and duration; unstressed /a/ is reduced toward [ə]

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed /a/ tends to [ə]; other vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: As for ps: strong dynamic stress, no instrumental rhythm study cited.

length.notes: As for ps: /ɑ/ is inherently longer than /a/ and /ə/; a length contrast in i and u is marginal; gemination is not contrastive.

intonation.declarative: pitch peaks on the stressed syllables of the main words, final fall to low on the verb at the end of the sentence
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of the statement with a final rise; an initial particle (ɑjɑ) is optional
intonation.wh_question: question word stays in place and carries the main accent; the utterance ends with a fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of a non-final phrase or clause
intonation.accent_shape: high or rising pitch on the stressed syllable
intonation.notes: Instrumental work on Pashto intonation is sparse and none is known to me for this dialect; this follows the reference grammars.

problems: the dialect is made by four phoneme replacements on the base ps voice (S. to C, Z. to J^, ts to s, dz to z); vowels, stress, word list and rules are those of ps, so every problem listed in the ps profile applies (missing short vowels in ps_list, final ی read as [iː], alveolar and aspirated stops, retroflexion by transitions only)
څ is turned into [s]; MacKenzie's table as usually reproduced keeps the affricate [ts] in the northwest and has the fricative only for ځ, so this replacement is doubtful
خ and غ stay uvular [χ ʁ]
good: ښ is the palatal [ç] and ږ the palatal [ʝ], taken from the base table's palatal fricatives, and ځ is [z], as described for this dialect

notes: Dialect groups by the pronunciation of five letters (MacKenzie 1959; Henderson 1983; Elfenbein 1997; David 2014). Southwest (Kandahar): ښ [ʂ], ږ [ʐ], څ [ts], ځ [dz], ژ [ʒ]. Southeast (Quetta): ښ [ʃ], ږ [ʒ]. Northwest (central Ghilzai): ښ [ç], ږ [ʝ], ځ [z]. Northeast (Yusufzai): ښ [x], ږ [ɡ], څ [s], ځ [z], ژ [dʒ]. The voice is marked 'status testing'.
